t: What Plastic Zip Ties Are and How They Lock
title: What Plastic Zip Ties Are and How They Lock
description: A plastic zip tie (cable tie) is a nylon strap with angled teeth on one side and a locking head with a one-way pawl: thread the tail through the head and it cinches tight, and the pawl stops it loosening. They are cheap, strong, and permanent — the standard for cable bundles you will never change. Standard ties are nylon 6/6, which gives them their strength and their weakness to UV.

demo.program:
print("Anatomy: nylon strap + angled teeth + locking head with one-way pawl.")
print("Thread tail through head: cinches tight, pawl blocks loosening.")
print("Standard material: nylon 6/6 (strong; UV-degrades outdoors).")
print("Use for: bundles you will NEVER change.")

t: Sizes, Lengths, and Tensile Strength Ratings
title: Sizes, Lengths, and Tensile Strength Ratings
description: Zip ties are sold by length and tensile strength: 4-inch ties rated around 18 lbs for thin wire bundles, 8-inch at 40-50 lbs as the general PC size, 12-inch at 50-75 lbs for thick PSU trunks, and heavy 120-lb ties for structural jobs. Width tracks strength — wider tie, stronger lock. For PC interiors, 8-inch 50-lb ties cover nearly everything; buy an assortment and you will reach for the 8-inch size nine times in ten.

demo.program:
ties = [("4 in", 18, "thin wire bundles"), ("8 in", 50, "general PC (the default)"),
        ("12 in", 75, "thick PSU trunks"), ("14 in heavy", 120, "structural")]
for l, lbs, use in ties:
    print(f"  {l:<12} {lbs:>3} lb -> {use}")
print("PC interiors: 8-in 50-lb covers ~everything. Assortment = mostly 8-in.")

t: Natural vs UV-Black Ties: Indoor and Outdoor Grades
title: Natural vs UV-Black Ties: Indoor and Outdoor Grades
description: Natural (white/clear) nylon ties are the indoor default; black ties add carbon black for UV resistance and survive years in sunlight. Outdoors or near windows, always use UV-rated black — natural ties go brittle and snap within a year or two of sun. Indoors the difference does not matter, so buy natural for the bench and black for anything sun-exposed. Stainless steel ties exist for heat and extreme duty, far beyond PC needs.

demo.program:
print("Natural (white): indoor default, cheapest.")
print("UV-black: carbon-black stabilized, years in sunlight. Use near windows/outdoors.")
print("Natural in sun: brittle and snapping within 1-2 years.")
print("Stainless: extreme heat/duty (overkill for PC work).")

t: Cinching Technique: Tight Enough, Never Crushing
title: Cinching Technique: Tight Enough, Never Crushing
description: Pull a zip tie snug — the bundle should not slide — then stop; one more hard yank deforms cable insulation and can pinch conductors. The pro move is a zip-tie gun (tensioning tool) that pulls to a set tension and cuts the tail flush automatically, giving identical ties every time. By hand, tighten, wiggle-test the bundle, and cut the tail. A tie that dents the cable jacket is too tight.

demo.program:
print("Snug = bundle doesn't slide. STOP there.")
print("Over-tight: dents jacket, pinches conductors (one more yank too many).")
print("Pro: tensioning gun -> set tension + auto flush-cut, identical every time.")
print("Hand method: tighten, wiggle-test, cut tail. Dented jacket = too tight.")

t: Use Case: Permanent Hidden Runs Behind the Motherboard Tray
title: Use Case: Permanent Hidden Runs Behind the Motherboard Tray
description: Zip ties earn their place on permanent hidden runs: the main PSU trunk behind the motherboard tray, in a case you do not plan to rewire. Strap the trunk to the tray's tie points with 8-inch ties, spaced 6 inches, tails trimmed flush. Because the run is hidden and permanent, the ties' single-use nature never matters — and the bundle will still be tight in five years.

n = trunk // spacing + 1
print(f"{trunk}-in hidden trunk: {n} ties at {spacing}-in spacing, tails flush.")
print("Use case rule: hidden + permanent = zip ties' home turf.")
print("If you might reroute it: velcro instead. No exceptions.")

t: Use Case: Fan Grills, Filters, and Case Mod Mounting
title: Use Case: Fan Grills, Filters, and Case Mod Mounting
description: Zip ties mount things, not just cables: fan filters to fan frames, LED strips along case edges, pump brackets in custom loops, and replacement fan grills. Four small ties through a fan's corner holes make a secure filter mount that pops off for cleaning. For mounting, use the tie's head as the anchor side and keep tension moderate — the tie holds position, it does not need to crush.

print("Head side = anchor. Moderate tension: hold position, don't crush.")

t: Releasable Zip Ties: The Reusable Exception
title: Releasable Zip Ties: The Reusable Exception
description: Releasable (reusable) zip ties have a small tab on the head that lifts the pawl, letting you open and reuse the tie dozens of times. They cost more and the tab can snag, but for test benches and prototyping they give zip-tie strength with velcro-like reversibility. Keep a bag of releasables on the test bench and single-use ties in the build kit — each where its traits pay off.

demo.program:
print("Releasable ties: tab lifts the pawl -> open + reuse dozens of times.")
print("Trade-off: cost more, tab can snag.")
print("Test bench: releasables (strength + reversibility).")
print("Build kit: single-use (cheap, permanent).")

title: Mounting-Head and Screw-Mount Ties
description: Mounting-head ties have a hole in the head for a screw, turning any surface into an anchor point; screw-mount the head to the case or desk, then cinch the bundle. Push-mount ties snap into chassis holes. These turn zip ties from bundle-wrappers into routed infrastructure — the bundle follows the mounts instead of floating. A row of screw-mount ties along a desk edge is a permanent cable raceway for dollars.

t: Cutting Tails: Flush Cutters vs Dikes vs the Twist
title: Cutting Tails: Flush Cutters vs Dikes vs the Twist
description: Trim tails flush with the head using flush cutters — angled snips leave a razor edge that slices fingers during the next build. Never twist-ties off: twisting work-hardens the nylon and leaves a sharp spike. Cut straight across at the head face, then run a finger over it; if it scratches, cut closer or file it. The next person to reach into the case will thank you.

demo.program:
print("Flush cutters: cut straight across at the head face (safe edge).")
print("Angled snips: leave a razor edge (slices fingers next build).")
print("NEVER twist off: work-hardens nylon into a sharp spike.")
print("Test: run a finger over it. Scratches = cut closer.")

t: Zip Tie Maintenance: Inspection and Replacement Cycles
title: Zip Tie Maintenance: Inspection and Replacement Cycles
description: Nylon ages: indoor ties last many years, but heat (near radiators, in hot cases) and UV embrittle them. Inspect yearly — flex a tie; if it snaps instead of bending, replace the batch. In hot cases (GPUs dumping heat nearby), prefer releasable ties or velcro for anything you will touch again, and keep single-use ties to cool hidden runs. A failed tie in a PSU trunk lets cables sag onto fans.

demo.program:
print("Yearly flex test: bends = good, snaps = replace the batch.")
print("Heat + UV embrittle nylon. Hot case zones: prefer velcro/releasables.")
print("Failed tie in PSU trunk -> cables sag onto fans. Inspect hidden runs too.")

t: Zip Ties vs Velcro vs Lacing Cord
title: Zip Ties vs Velcro vs Lacing Cord
description: Zip ties: cheapest, strongest, permanent, need cutters. Velcro: reusable, gentle, costs more, weaker hold. Lacing cord (waxed twine, the old telecom method): beautiful, strong, reusable with skill, but slow to apply. For PC work the practical split is velcro for anything changeable and zip ties for permanent hidden runs; lacing cord is for show builds and restorations where the craft is the point.

demo.program:
print("zip tie    : cheap, strong, permanent, needs cutters")
print("velcro     : reusable, gentle, pricier, weaker")
print("lacing cord: beautiful, strong, slow (show builds, restorations)")
print("PC split: velcro for changeable, zip ties for permanent hidden runs.")

t: Advanced: The Double-Tie and Cross-Tie for Heavy Trunks
title: Advanced: The Double-Tie and Cross-Tie for Heavy Trunks
description: Heavy PSU trunks defeat single ties over time — nylon creeps under constant load. The double-tie puts two ties side by side sharing the load; the cross-tie loops a second tie perpendicular through the first's head, anchoring the bundle against sliding along its axis. For 1000W-plus cable sets behind the tray, double-ties every 6 inches hold for years where singles eventually loosen.

demo.program:
print("Double-tie: two ties side by side, load shared (beats nylon creep).")
print("Cross-tie: second tie perpendicular through first head (blocks axial slide).")
print("1000W+ trunks: double-ties every 6 in hold for years.")

t: Specialty Ties: Beaded, Stainless, and Detectable
title: Specialty Ties: Beaded, Stainless, and Detectable
description: Beaded ties (ladder-style, no pawl) release and reuse — handy for temporary bundling. Stainless steel ties handle exhaust-heat zones and outdoor masts where nylon dies. Metal-detectable blue ties serve food and cleanroom-adjacent work. For PC building, beaded ties are the useful specialty — a bag of them replaces tape for temporary holds during test fits.

title: The Complete Zip-Tie Discipline
description: The master discipline: 8-inch 50-lb as the default, snug-never-crushing tension, tails cut flush with proper cutters, double-ties on heavy trunks, releasables on the test bench, mounting-heads for anchored runs, yearly flex-test inspections, and velcro anywhere change is possible. Zip ties are permanent — the discipline is deciding, before each tie, whether 'permanent' is really what this bundle wants.

        "double-ties on heavy trunks", "releasables on test bench",
        "mounting-heads for anchors", "yearly flex inspection",
        "velcro anywhere change is possible"]
for i, d in enumerate(disc, 1):
    print(f"  {i}. {d}")
print("Core question before each tie: is 'permanent' really what this bundle wants?")
